client: I've been really struggling lately with this new job I started at a tech startup about a month ago. The hours are brutal — I'm staying late almost every night, and by the time I get home I'm completely drained but I can't even sleep properly because my mind keeps racing about everything I still need to get done. Honestly, I'm not sure talking about it is going to change the fact that there's just too much work and not enough hours in the day.
therapist: What you're describing sounds genuinely exhausting — that cycle of pushing through long days and then not even getting the rest you need because your mind won't quiet down is really draining on every level. I also notice you came here even while doubting it would help, and I'm curious about that — what made you decide to reach out today despite that skepticism?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess I just got to a point where I was tired enough to try anything, even something I wasn't sure about. The nights where I lie there replaying every mistake I made at work, every awkward thing I said, every way I let someone down — it's been getting worse lately, not better. I don't know, maybe part of me hoped someone could just tell me how to make my brain shut up long enough to actually sleep.
therapist: That nightly replay of mistakes and missteps sounds truly exhausting — like your mind is running a highlight reel of everything that went wrong, just when you most need it to rest. What you're describing, that relentless self-scrutiny, is something we can actually work with directly in CBT, because often those replays are driven by thoughts that feel like facts but aren't quite the whole picture. Can you tell me a little more about what kinds of thoughts tend to show up most — is it more about worrying what others think of you, or more of an inner critic telling you that you're not measuring up?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: It's honestly both, but if I had to pick the one that hits hardest, it's the inner critic thing. Like, I'll be lying there and suddenly remember something I said in a meeting three weeks ago, and this voice just jumps in and says "see, that's why people don't take you seriously." And then I start spiraling about whether my coworkers actually respect me or if they're just being polite to my face.
therapist: That inner critic sounds incredibly harsh — taking one moment from weeks ago and turning it into a sweeping verdict about your worth in other people's eyes is such a heavy thing to carry, especially at 2am when there's nothing to push back against it. What's interesting is that the critic's "evidence" is usually pretty one-sided — it collects the awkward moments but tends to ignore the times things went well. I'm wondering, if a trusted friend described how they saw you showing up at work, do you think their version would match what that inner voice is telling you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, I don't know... maybe their version would be a little kinder, but I'm not sure I'd actually believe it even if they said it. Like, I feel like people are just being polite when they say nice things, and the awkward moments are the ones that are "real." It's hard to trust the positive stuff when the negative feels so much louder and more certain.
therapist: You've just named something really important — this idea that negative feedback is "the truth" while positive feedback is just politeness is actually a well-recognized thinking pattern called discounting the positive, and it's incredibly common but also incredibly unfair to yourself. It's like your mind has set up a system where the critic can never lose — bad moments count as proof, and good moments get dismissed as noise. I'm curious, when did you first start feeling like the negative version of yourself was the more "real" one — does that go back further than this job?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. I think it goes back pretty far — like maybe middle school, when I started feeling like I was always on the outside of things, like everyone else had some manual I never got. I remember getting decent grades but always focusing on the one subject I struggled with, thinking that was the "real" picture of how smart I was.
therapist: That image of a kid who got decent grades but zeroed in on the one struggle as the "real truth" — that's such a clear early version of the same pattern that's keeping you up at night now, and it makes a lot of sense that it would feel so deeply ingrained. It sounds like you learned pretty early that belonging and being "enough" felt uncertain, and your mind developed this habit of treating the hard moments as the most reliable data. I'm wondering, what do you think that younger version of you most needed to hear back then that they weren't getting?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. I think that kid needed someone to just... notice him without there being a catch, like "you're doing okay and I see you" without it being tied to a performance or a grade or anything. But even saying that out loud feels a little embarrassing, like I'm being dramatic or asking for too much.
therapist: What you just described — needing to be seen simply for who you are, not for what you produce — is one of the most fundamental human needs there is, and there's nothing dramatic about that at all. And yet I notice that even as you said something really vulnerable and true, you immediately moved to minimize it, almost like that inner critic jumped in right on cue to call it "too much." What would it feel like to just let that need be valid, without the disclaimer?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean... I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to just accept that, but it's like the moment I try to let the need be valid, something in me goes "okay but who are you to need that?" It feels almost dangerous to just sit with it without immediately explaining it away or making it smaller. I guess I'm scared that if I actually believe I deserve to be seen, and then I'm still not... that would hurt so much more than if I'd just kept my expectations low.
therapist: What you just said is so honest and so human — that keeping expectations low feels like protection, like if you never fully believe you deserve to be seen, you can't be devastated when it doesn't happen. But I notice there's something almost urgent in how you're saying this, like this isn't just an intellectual idea but something that feels very alive and close right now. That fear of hoping and then being disappointed — has there been a specific moment in your life where you did let yourself believe you deserved to be seen, and then it didn't happen?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, there was one time. I had this friend, someone I thought actually got me, and I opened up about some stuff I'd never told anyone — like real stuff, not just surface-level complaints. And then she just kind of... drifted away after that, started being less available, and I never really got an explanation, so I've spent a long time wondering if it was because of what I shared.
therapist: That experience sounds like it left a really deep mark — you took a genuine risk, let someone truly see you, and then lost them without ever knowing why, which means part of you has been quietly carrying the weight of "maybe it was my fault for sharing too much." The way you're telling this, there's something very still and careful about it, like it's still tender even now. I want to ask gently — do you think that friendship is where the rule "staying small is safer than being seen" really took hold?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, I think you're probably right about that, even though it's uncomfortable to admit it. That friendship was the first time I really let someone in, and when it just... ended, with no explanation, I think some part of me decided the vulnerability itself was the problem. It's like I drew this conclusion that if I hadn't shared so much, I wouldn't have gotten hurt, and that's been running quietly in the background ever since.
therapist: You've just uncovered something really significant — that your mind took one painful, unexplained loss and turned it into a rule about vulnerability itself being dangerous, when the truth is that her drifting away said nothing certain about what you shared or who you are. That quiet conclusion has been doing a lot of work in the background, shaping how much of yourself you let people see ever since. I'm wondering, now that you can see that rule more clearly, does it still feel as true as it once did — or does some part of you recognize it might have been a hurt child's way of making sense of something that was never really explained?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me does recognize that... like, intellectually I can see the logic of it. But it doesn't quite feel as simple as just realizing the rule is wrong, because that feeling of "don't let people too close" has been protecting me for so long that I'm not sure I'd even know how to function without it. It's like you're asking me to walk around without armor, and even if the armor is heavy and uncomfortable, at least I know what it feels like to wear it.
therapist: The armor metaphor you used is really perfect, and I want to honor it — you're not being asked to just throw it off, because something that's kept you safe for that long deserves to be set down slowly and carefully, not ripped away. And even as you're describing this so thoughtfully, there's something in how you're speaking that sounds a little quieter, a little more fragile than your words alone convey, like this is landing somewhere deeper than just an intellectual realization. What does it feel like in your body right now, sitting with all of this?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech
